📊 Visa finds 46% in Asia Pacific may use stablecoins by 2031 

📣 Stablecoin interest has moved well ahead of actual use across Asia Pacific, with 46% of surveyed consumers saying they are likely to use the tokens within five years compared with 16% who used them during the past year. The research found strong interest in using stablecoins for online purchases, travel, overseas shopping and moving money across borders. Yet the survey showed a large knowledge gap, with only 6% of respondents demonstrating what Visa described as an accurate understanding of how stablecoins work.

⭐️ Across the 14 markets, 46% of respondents said they were likely to use stablecoins during the next five years. Only 16% reported using them during the previous 12 months. Visa did not disclose in its release what those existing users had used stablecoins for. The 16% figure could therefore include trading, transfers, payments or other cryptocurrency activity and should not be treated solely as consumer payment adoption.

‼️ Cross-border transfers produced one of the strongest future-use readings. Around 49% of respondents said they thought stablecoins could become a common method of moving money between countries within five years. Visa Head of Digital Currencies for Asia Pacific Nischint Sanghavi said consumers were starting to consider stablecoins for “online purchases, travel and cross-border transfers.” The company views those uses as potential extensions of existing payment behavior.

➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

💬 Iran opens first children’s cancer diagnosis and treatment center

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran has inaugurated its first university-based center for the diagnosis and treatment of childhood cancer at Hakim Children’s Hospital in Tehran, with Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref and Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarghandi in attendance.

The center was inaugurated on Thursday, coinciding with World Children’s Day, in a ceremony also attended by Mohammad Eslami, vice president and head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, and a number of Health Ministry officials.
​
Aref and Zafarghandi visited the hospital’s inpatient wards and met with children receiving treatment and their families.
​
Speaking at the ceremony, Tehran University of Medical Sciences Chancellor Reza Raeis-Karami said the opening of the center could play an effective role in reducing out-of-pocket medical expenses for families.
​
“Today is an important day ahead of us, because we have two important projects,” Raeis-Karami said, referring to the inauguration of the children’s cancer center and the launch of construction of the 320-bed Amir Alam 2 Hospital.
​
He described the comprehensive center for the diagnosis and treatment of childhood cancer as a turning point for the country, noting that services in this field had previously been provided only by the private sector.
​
“With the opening of this center, the first university-based and public center in the field of childhood cancer treatment begins its activities,” he added.

McDonald’s has rolled out a system that calculates how much people are willing to pay for a specific item.

It looks at millions of orders, competitors’ prices, and how customers respond to price increases. If people at one location are willing to pay more for a Big Mac without hesitation, the algorithm takes that into account.

A real-world example:
At two McDonald’s locations just 3 km apart, a Big Mac can cost $5.69 and $6.89. That’s a 21% difference.

Online retailers are already using the same approach: in the US, in 74% of cases, the same product is shown to different people at different prices.

AI takes into account purchase history, abandoned carts, time spent on a page, even mouse movements, and dozens of other factors.

According to research, personalized pricing is already generating 19% more profit for companies. So it looks like this is what sales will increasingly be built around.
